notes.buffer.durability: the only tier implemented; `disk` is refused by name
notes.buffer.flush:
Three triggers, and whichever is crossed FIRST sends the batch.

`size` is the newest and the reason is memory rather than throughput:
the other two are counts, and a count cannot tell 500 events of 2 KB
from 500 of 2 MB. Every flush is counted by what triggered it --
brevis_gateway_flushes_total{trigger="time|records|size"} -- because
on a BigQuery stream a size flush firing routinely means the
60-second floor is being walked past and the daily load-job quota
with it.
notes.buffer.flush.max_age:
The age at which a partial batch goes REGARDLESS.

`every` is a TARGET and this is a PROMISE, and the difference will
matter once the flush claim lands (issue #36): a replica that loses
a window to another keeps filling, so the target can be deferred.
This cannot be -- no event waits longer, whatever the contention,
even with the metastore unreachable.

The gap between the two is how much contention this deployment
tolerates. It has to be at least `every`; a ceiling under the target
would mean the target never applies, and the config refuses it.

It also settles the drain: what a buffer can be HOLDING at SIGTERM
is bounded by this, not by `every`, so the grace period the gateway
prints at boot is derived from it.
notes.buffer.max_bytes:
And the same ceiling in BYTES, which is the one that stops an OOM.

A count cannot see it: 10,000 records is 20 MB of 2 KB events and
20 GB of 2 MB ones, and until this field existed the file had no way
to say which this stream holds. Measured on what ARRIVED -- a
map[string]any weighs several times its JSON, and a hook that inflates
an event is not counted. It has to be at least listen.max_body, or one
request could never be admitted.
notes.buffer.workers:
Delivery is asynchronous and bounded. A request appends to the buffer
and returns; a full batch is handed to one of these workers, so no
caller ever waits for a publish, a COPY, or a sink that is down.

workers     how many batches are delivered at once
queue       how many full batches may wait for a worker
max_records the ceiling on events held in memory for this stream.
            Past it the gateway answers 503 rather than accepting an
            event it has nowhere to put -- and the 503 is safe to act
            on: send the same body again, the ingestion_id is a frozen
            function of the event, so a retry is the same record.
notes.dead_letter:
Where a batch the sink will not take goes. Required, not defaulted: a
stream without one loses a refused batch to a log line, and an operator
who never chose that does not know it is happening.

`files` reads a directory, gs:// and s3://, so this is a folder on a
laptop and a bucket in production with no change to the gateway.

Each record carries _dead_letter_reason, _dead_letter_sink and
_dead_letter_at: whoever finds this file has the events and not the log,
and "why is this here" is their first question.
notes.format: json | array | ndjson -- declared, never sniffed
notes.hook: A name in this binary's registry, not a path. Hooks are Go, compiled in.
notes.identity:
What becomes the ingestion_id. All four, because the formula is frozen
over exactly these: leaving one out produces a DIFFERENT id, not a
weaker one. provider and entity are the stream's; source_key and
record_ts name fields of the event.
notes.oversize:
The claim check: an event too big is written somewhere WHOLE, and a
reduced version continues carrying a pointer back to it.

A flat 413 loses the event, and an oversized payload is usually the most
interesting one somebody has -- the request with the whole document
attached, which is the case worth debugging.

`larger_than` measures one EVENT, after the hook. listen.max_body is a
different thing: it caps a whole REQUEST and refuses with 413 before a
byte is parsed.

`hook` names a second hook that returns the reduced event. Which fields
are heavy is domain knowledge and a YAML file cannot hold it. WITHOUT
one, the event is archived and dropped from the stream -- not lost,
because the archive has it whole, and counted, because an event that
silently stops arriving is the worst outcome here.
notes.retry:
How hard the sink is tried before a batch is given up on. Four attempts
over roughly seven seconds: enough to ride out a restart on the other
side, short enough that a sink which is down is known to be down.
notes.sink.attributes:
Fields of the EVENT that travel as message attributes. The topic's
contract belongs to whoever owns the topic, so nothing is invented here.
notes.stamp_loaded_at:
Writes ingestion_loaded_at: when the gateway received it, UTC, RFC3339.
The SDK's column and the SDK's format, so a row this gateway lands and a
row a pipeline lands are the same shape. Opt-in, because it adds a field
and both a topic's subscribers and a table's columns notice.

notes:
The same events into a table, which is the other half of what a gateway is
for: one stream feeds whoever subscribes, another lands what somebody will
query.
notes.format: one object per line: a batch in one request
notes.sink.dsn_from:
The NAME of the environment variable holding the connection string,
never the string: a DSN carries a password and this file is in git.
notes.sink.table:
Schema-qualified. The table must exist -- this does not create one,
because a service that creates tables turns a typo here into a second
table nobody is reading.
notes.sink.write:
Required, never defaulted. The two are genuinely different and only
the table's owner knows which it is:

  append  COPY FROM STDIN, Postgres's fast path. Every delivery lands,
          including a redelivery. Right for a log, wrong for a table
          somebody counts.
  merge   the batch staged in a TEMP table and inserted with
          ON CONFLICT (ingestion_id) DO NOTHING, all in ONE
          transaction. The FIRST delivery wins and a redelivery is
          ignored. Needs a UNIQUE index on ingestion_id, and the
          driver refuses without one rather than silently appending:

            CREATE UNIQUE INDEX CONCURRENTLY ON landing.orders (ingestion_id)

`upsert` -- ON CONFLICT DO UPDATE, where the LAST delivery wins -- is
refused by name. It is a real mode nobody has implemented yet, and
accepting the word while behaving like `merge` is the failure this
field exists to prevent.

notes:
BigQuery. No dsn_from: it authenticates with the pod's own credentials,
which is what a workload identity is for. A connection string here would be
a second way to do what the platform already does.
notes.dead_letter.type:
The dead letter in a bucket, which is what it should be in production:
written inside the image it would die with the container. Needs the
pod's GCP credentials, resolved at startup rather than on the first
batch it has to bury.
notes.format: a JSON array of objects in one request
notes.sink.table:
No dots: for BigQuery the project and the dataset are their own fields,
so "landing.telemetry" here would make a table with that literal name.

notes:
One route, N tables, nothing declared.

The producer POSTs an ENVELOPE: control fields at the top, the record
inside `data`.

  {
    "table_name": "app_orders",     <- required
    "unique_key": "id",             <- optional, default "id"; the FIELD
                                       it names must be in `data`, and
                                       `write: merge` requires one at all
    "operation":  "INSERT",         <- optional: INSERT | UPDATE | DELETE
    "description": "Pedidos",       <- optional, and READ BY NOTHING today:
                                       it is in the contract for the
                                       console page that does not exist
    "data": {                       <- required: the record, and only it
      "id": "A-3",
      "total": 150,
      "customer": {"id": 7, "uf": "SP"}
    }
  }

Every table carries the same seven columns whatever the record holds:

  brevis_ingestion_id   the identity; the merge key
  brevis_record_key     data[unique_key] -- which ROW this is about.
                        NULL under `append`, where a log line need not be
                        about a record at all; required by `merge`, which
                        keeps one row per record
  brevis_operation      INSERT | UPDATE | DELETE
  brevis_received_at    OUR clock, at the 202 -- the partition column
  brevis_loaded_at      DEFAULT CURRENT_TIMESTAMP -- the destination stamps it
  brevis_stream         which route wrote it
  brevis_gateway        which deployment
  brevis_received_bytes how large the event arrived, envelope included --
                        free, because buffer.flush.size already counts it.
                        INGRESS and not storage: the destination keeps the
                        row typed and compressed, so 400 bytes of JSON may
                        be 80 on disk. Summing it answers "which table is
                        growing, since when, from whom" -- which the
                        metrics cannot, because they carry no `table`
                        label and that label is the producer's to choose.

`brevis_` is RESERVED: a `data` carrying any key with it is refused per
event, because otherwise a producer forges a control field -- and a forged
brevis_received_at is worse than none, since it looks real.

UPDATE and DELETE are RECORDED, never applied. A landing table is history,
and resolving "the current version of each record" is the downstream
model's job:

  qualify row_number() over (partition by brevis_record_key
                             order by brevis_received_at desc) = 1
     and brevis_operation <> 'DELETE'
notes.buffer.flush.claim:
The flush clock belongs to the DEPLOYMENT, not to each process.

Without this, `every` is a time.AfterFunc in every replica, so the
load jobs a table receives are `replicas × 86400 / every` -- on
BigQuery, against 1,500 per table per DAY, two replicas at 60s is
already 192% of a quota that cannot be raised. The gateway scales out
for HTTP concurrency while the sink wants concentration.

With it, a replica takes a set-if-absent claim for the stream and the
window before flushing on the timer, and the timer wakes on the
window BOUNDARY so every replica asks for the same key. One flush per
window, whatever the replica count -- and it self-adjusts, because a
replica only waits when another is actually competing.

Needs a SHARED metastore. With `memory` every replica wins its own
claim and nothing coordinates. And it needs `max_age`, which the
config refuses without: the claim turns `every` into a target, and a
target with no ceiling is latency with nothing bounding it.

A metastore that is unreachable flushes anyway. Losing coordination
costs load jobs; refusing to flush holds data.

Watch brevis_gateway_flush_windows_total{outcome}:

  won | yielded     the feature working -- one flushes, the rest fill
  ceiling           max_age did it, not the target
  unreachable       ALERT. The backend could not be asked, so the
                    claim failed open and the jobs are multiplying by
                    replica count again -- silently, because every
                    flush still looks like a flush

The claim gives EXCLUSIVITY, not fairness: whoever asks first wins,
and a real two-replica run measured 4/1 rather than an even split.
`max_age` is what stops the unlucky one starving. Issue #36.

The claim's key carries the TABLE, because the flush trigger does
(issue #38): two replicas behind a load balancer do not hold the
same tables, and one claim for the stream would make one table's
cadence another's.

A window therefore asks for one claim per table. Redis answers them
in one round trip; every other backend answers them in parallel,
bounded. Measured at 94 tables against a backend 25ms away: 89ms on
memcached, 30ms on Redis. Both inside the 500ms the claim is given,
and memcached is the slower choice rather than a refused one.
notes.buffer.flush.every:
60s, not 1s: BigQuery allows 1,500 load jobs per table per DAY, and
a one-second window is 86,400. The config refuses anything shorter.
notes.buffer.flush.max_age: Five minutes of latency bought for job economy, and bounded.
notes.buffer.flush.size:
A CEILING here and not a target, and nothing refuses a smaller one
because the arrival rate is not knowable at load. The floor above
governs the TIMER; a size that fires every few seconds walks right
past it and spends the same daily quota. Watch
brevis_gateway_flushes_total{trigger="size"} on this stream: above
zero, it is telling you the window is not what is batching.
notes.sink.metastore:
The shared state this stream keeps: a cache of what tables exist, the
debounce that keeps N replicas from all running the same DDL, the
counter behind max_new_per_hour -- and, from issue #36, the claim that
makes the flush clock belong to the deployment rather than to each
process.

It is a STREAM's, not a sink's, even though it is written under one.
Every stream gets it, whatever the sink -- so a `bigquery` stream
without `auto_table` can name one too, and is validated the same way.

`memory` is the default and needs nothing. With ONE replica it is the
right answer. With several it gives each its own, so the debounce
debounces nothing and max_new_per_hour bounds a process -- which is
what redis and memcached are for, and the only reason they exist here.

`addr_from` is the NAME of the environment variable holding the
address, never the address: it carries a password often enough.
notes.sink.metastore.ttl:
How long the cache may be WRONG. `0` means never, and saying
nothing takes the sixty-second default -- three states, which is
why the field is a pointer in the config.

The clock is NOT what recovers from a wrong entry. A write the
destination refuses calls `invalidate`, which drops the entry at
once and lets the pipe's own retry come back against a cold cache:
a table dropped by hand costs one failed attempt, not a minute.

Expiry has a price, though. `sinkFor` charges
`naming.max_new_per_hour` when it does not KNOW a table -- so a miss
charges for a table that has existed for weeks, and a pod restarting
a minute after a table's last event gets nothing from the shared
store it is paying for. `ttl: 0` is the answer when the tables are
long-lived. See issue #35.
notes.sink.naming.max_new_per_hour:
Shared across replicas here, because the metastore below is redis.
Under `memory` it is PER REPLICA and four of them admit four times
this. A circuit breaker either way, not a quota: it bounds
creations, never writes.
notes.sink.shape:
What the RECORD contributes to the row.

  document  data goes whole into one JSON column. No DDL, ever, after
            the create: a new field is a new key.
  columns   each field gets a column -- scalars STRING, objects and
            arrays JSON. The shape people picture, and the one that
            pays for itself with DDL, quota and a write-stream reopen.

No type inference either way. A field that arrives whole today and
fractional tomorrow would change a column with nobody writing
anything; typing one is the PROMOTION path, written in this file and
reviewed in a diff.
